summary: Psalm 94 begins by calling on Yahweh, the judge of the earth, to answer proud and violent evildoers. The poem describes the wicked crushing Yahweh’s people, argues that the maker of ear and eye surely hears and sees, then turns to the comfort and help the speaker has received. It ends by contrasting corrupt rule with Yahweh as refuge and by expecting the wicked to be cut off by their own wickedness.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows Book IV of Psalms praying for God’s rule in a world where violent people and unjust authorities seem to prosper. It holds together protest, moral reasoning, personal testimony, and trust without pretending the crisis is small.

context.author: No individual author is named in the chapter. Psalms as a whole is a many-voiced anthology associated with several writers and collections.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: The Psalter contains poems and collections from different periods; assigning one date to Psalm 94 is not established by the chapter.
context.setting: Book IV of Psalms, within a collection that often relocates security from fragile human power to God’s kingship, justice, and refuge.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic prayer: complaint, accusation, wisdom-like instruction, testimony, and confidence in God as judge and refuge.

outline.heading: Call for judgment
outline.note: The speaker appeals to Yahweh as the God to whom vengeance belongs and as judge of the earth.

outline.heading: What the wicked do
outline.note: The wicked boast, crush Yahweh’s people, kill the vulnerable, and claim that God does not see or consider.

outline.heading: God sees and knows
outline.note: The poem rebukes the foolish by arguing that the one who made the ear and eye must hear and see, and that Yahweh knows human thoughts.

outline.heading: Instruction and future rest
outline.note: The blessed person is taught by Yahweh, and the poem affirms that Yahweh will not forsake his people and that judgment will return to righteousness.

outline.heading: Personal rescue and comfort
outline.note: The speaker asks who will stand against evildoers, then remembers Yahweh’s help, loving kindness, and comforts.

outline.heading: Corrupt power and refuge
outline.note: The psalm denies fellowship between God and a wicked throne, describes the innocent condemned, and ends with Yahweh as refuge who cuts off wickedness.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh, you God to whom vengeance belongs, you God to whom vengeance belongs, shine out.
keyVerses.why: This opening names the psalm’s central appeal: vengeance is placed with Yahweh, not with the speaker.

keyVerses.text: He who implanted the ear, won’t he hear? He who formed the eye, won’t he see?
keyVerses.why: This verse answers the claim that God does not notice injustice by reasoning from God as maker of human perception.

keyVerses.text: For Yahweh won’t reject his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the psalm’s confidence after its complaint about Yahweh’s people being crushed.

keyVerses.text: But Yahweh has been my high tower, my God, the rock of my refuge.
keyVerses.why: This turns the poem’s public cry for justice into personal testimony about Yahweh as protection.

themes: God as judge of the earth
The folly of thinking God does not see

questions.question: Why does the psalm ask for vengeance?
questions.answer: The opening asks Yahweh, the God to whom vengeance belongs, to shine out and repay the proud. In this chapter, vengeance is framed as God’s judicial action against people who boast, crush Yahweh’s people, and kill the vulnerable. The psalm is not a private permission slip for revenge; it is a prayer handing judgment to God.

questions.question: Who are the wicked in this psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter describes them by actions rather than by names. They speak arrogantly, boast, break Yahweh’s people in pieces, afflict his heritage, and kill the widow, the alien, and the fatherless. Later the psalm also connects wickedness with a throne that brings about mischief by statute.

questions.question: What does “heritage” mean here?
questions.answer: In verse 5, “heritage” is parallel to “your people,” so it refers to the people who belong to Yahweh in the poem’s language. Verse 14 uses a related idea when it says Yahweh will not forsake “his inheritance.” The point is relational: the victims are not invisible or ownerless before God.

questions.question: Why does verse 7 matter so much?
questions.answer: Verse 7 gives the wicked person’s claim: “Yah will not see, neither will Jacob’s God consider.” The next verses directly answer that claim by asking whether the one who made the ear and eye can fail to hear and see. The psalm’s argument turns on God’s awareness of what the wicked deny.

questions.question: Is “discipline” in verse 12 punishment?
questions.answer: The verse calls the disciplined person blessed because Yah teaches him out of his law. In this psalm, discipline is connected with instruction and with being given rest during days of adversity. It should not be reduced to punishment for wrongdoing, since the chapter contrasts the taught person with the wicked who face the pit.

questions.question: What does the psalm mean by “the pit is dug for the wicked”?
questions.answer: The phrase pictures coming downfall for the wicked while the taught person is given rest from adversity. The psalm does not describe the mechanics or timing of that downfall in detail. It speaks poetically about judgment becoming unavoidable, especially in light of the closing claim that Yahweh will cut them off in their own wickedness.

questions.question: Why does the speaker ask, “Who will rise up for me?”
questions.answer: The question in verse 16 expresses isolation in the face of wicked people and evildoers. Verse 17 answers from experience: without Yahweh’s help, the speaker says his soul would have soon lived in silence. The movement is from unanswered human support to remembered divine help.

questions.question: What kind of distress appears in verses 18-19?
questions.answer: The speaker describes instability with the cry, “My foot is slipping!” and inner turmoil as “the multitude of my thoughts within me.” The answer is not that the trouble never existed, but that Yahweh’s loving kindness held him up and Yahweh’s comforts delighted his soul. The psalm allows both danger and consolation to be named plainly.

questions.question: What is the “throne of wickedness”?
questions.answer: Verse 20 asks whether a throne of wickedness can have fellowship with God, and describes it as bringing about mischief by statute. That points to corrupt authority using law or decree to harm rather than protect. Readers differ on whether to connect this to a specific historical regime, but the chapter itself does not name one.

glossary.def: Judicial repayment or retribution. In this psalm it belongs to Yahweh, who is addressed as judge of the earth.
The people opposed to Yahweh’s justice in the chapter. They boast, harm Yahweh’s people, deny that God sees, and are finally said to be cut off in their own wickedness.
A socially vulnerable person named among those killed by the wicked in verse 6.
A foreigner or resident outsider named with the widow and fatherless as a target of violence in verse 6.
An image for protection and refuge. The speaker says Yahweh has been his high tower in verse 22.
